rationale: Start with a broad gradient to locate the elution window and critical pairs while minimizing the risk of missing strongly retained compounds. A midpoint temperature leaves room to explore temperature-dependent selectivity in either direction.

Change only gradient duration to test whether the crowded central peaks respond to a shallower slope. The initial last-peak time leaves room to improve resolution without exceeding the 10-minute scoring threshold.

The shallower gradient improved the critical pair substantially, leaving only one pair below baseline resolution. Raising temperature by 5 C tests selectivity at that pair while providing more margin below the 10-minute time threshold.

The critical pair converged sharply between 40 and 45 C, suggesting an elution-order crossover just above 45 C. Testing 60 C should move beyond that crossover to recover separation while further shortening retention.

An intermediate temperature should separate the new close pair at 60 C while retaining separation beyond the central-pair crossover. Slightly steepening the gradient may further help the reordered central pair and shorten the run.
Injection 5 achieved the maximum CRF; retain it as the benchmark. Shorten the gradient by one grid step to test whether full resolution can be maintained with a faster separation.

Trim the gradient window while restoring the successful injection 5 slope of 0.075 organic fraction per minute. This should shorten retention without the resolution loss caused by simply steepening the gradient, though the marginal pairs need verification.

Test a faster, higher-temperature regime that may carry the troublesome middle pair through an elution-order crossover and separate it on the other side. Injection 5 remains the maximum-score fallback if this compressed method loses resolution.

Keep injection 8's slope and temperature but raise the starting organic fraction to shift selectivity further beyond the middle-pair crossover. This tests a shorter fully resolved separation, while checking that the earliest peaks remain sufficiently retained and separated.

Lower the starting organic fraction to protect the early pair, and test a steeper gradient to increase separation of the middle pair after its order reversal. This explores a faster alternative while retaining injection 5 as the fully resolved benchmark.

Explore the cooler selectivity regime, since faster high-temperature methods have introduced competing critical pairs. Keeping the original gradient isolates the temperature effect and tests whether low-temperature elution-order changes offer another route to full resolution.

Return to the promising 40 C selectivity with approximately injection 2's gradient slope, but shift the window upward to shorten retention. This tests whether the window shift also improves the remaining critical pair without compressing the first two peaks excessively.

Make injection 12's gradient shallower to spread its remaining critical pair. The last peak previously exited near 0.61 organic fraction, so a 0.65 endpoint should still elute all compounds near the 10-minute scoring threshold.

Refine the faster 55 C regime by making injection 7's slope shallower while keeping its starting composition. This should improve the deficient middle pair and test whether both critical pairs can clear 1.5 with more balanced resolution.

Slightly flatten injection 14's gradient to seek more resolution margin at its two near-threshold pairs. The last peak should remain below 10 minutes, so improved robustness may be possible without sacrificing the maximum CRF.

Preserve injection 5's starting composition, temperature, and successful gradient slope while ending the ramp sooner. Its last peak exited near 0.57 organic fraction, so a 0.65 endpoint should retain full resolution and the maximum CRF with a shorter programmed gradient.

Shift the successful 55 C window upward while making the slope slightly shallower to compensate for the middle-pair compression seen at higher starting organic fraction. This tests whether a narrower window can preserve full resolution with earlier elution.

Lower injection 17's endpoint by one grid step to improve its sole unresolved pair while preserving the other separations. The expected increase in last-peak retention should still leave the run below the 10-minute penalty threshold.

One further endpoint reduction should lift injection 18's only deficient pair above 1.5 while keeping the last peak below 10 minutes. This targets another maximum-score method with potentially more balanced resolution margins than injection 5.

Test a shallower 60 C gradient to improve the middle pair that remained unresolved in injection 4, while maintaining the stronger central-pair separation at this temperature. The projected last-peak time is just below 10 minutes, potentially yielding full resolution with greater margin.

Test a smaller slope increase from the fastest fully resolved method than injection 6 attempted. This brackets the speed limit near injection 5, checking whether a slope of 0.080 can retain full resolution while shortening last-peak retention.

Use a slope between the fully resolved injections 14 and 15, with an endpoint above their estimated last-peak elution composition. This targets maximum CRF with modest resolution margin and a shorter programmed gradient.

Refine around injection 5 with a slightly shallower gradient to improve its middle-pair margin while checking that the other critical pair stays above 1.5. This should retain the maximum CRF with last-peak retention comfortably below 10 minutes.

Preserve the fastest fully resolved method's slope through the crowded peaks, then end the ramp earlier. This tests whether a 0.50-organic hold can elute the final compound within 10 minutes while retaining maximum CRF and reducing the endpoint solvent strength.

Slightly steepen the slope of fully resolved injection 19, targeting earlier last-peak elution while retaining its stronger resolution margins. Injection 5 remains the fastest demonstrated maximum-CRF method if this final refinement loses baseline resolution.
